case_prompt: A 52-year-old woman with obesity and chronic prednisone use for presumed pulmonary fibrosis initially presented to an urgent care center two days earlier for a presumed conjunctivitis and was prescribed polymyxin. She then came to the emergency department complaining that her head felt swollen and that her throat was beginning to swell. She self-administered her EpiPen® without improvement and was treated for possible anaphylaxis without benefit. On arrival, her blood pressure was 160/90 mm Hg, pulse 120 beats/min, temperature 36.8 °C, respiratory rate 22 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 100% on room air. Posterior oropharyngeal edema was noted. During her evaluation, she reported acute vision loss in the right eye and was transferred for ophthalmologic assessment. Over the next few hours, she developed severe bilateral periorbital swelling and chemosis. Extraocular motor testing initially showed right-sided ophthalmoplegia that progressed to bilateral cranial nerves III, IV, and VI palsies. Pupillary examination revealed relative afferent pupillary defects. Laboratory studies showed diabetic ketoacidosis attributed to chronic steroid use, a white blood cell count of 18,400 cells/μL with 96% neutrophils, and acute kidney injury. Noncontrast CT of the orbits and sinuses demonstrated right proptosis, right periorbital soft-tissue swelling, and mucosal thickening of all paranasal sinuses. Funduscopic examination revealed a retinal pattern consistent with right central retinal artery occlusion.

diagnostic_reasoning: 1. Conjunctivitis was initially considered — “was prescribed polymyxin for presumed conjunctivitis.” 2. Anaphylaxis was considered given the oropharyngeal edema and patient’s self‐report — “she believed she was having an allergic reaction; after using her EpiPen® without resolution, she came to the ED to be treated.” 3. Bacterial or viral sinusitis or orbital cellulitis would explain early periorbital swelling — “the initial symptoms of rhinocerebral mucormycosis are usually mistaken for bacterial or viral sinusitis or orbital cellulitis.” 4. Upper respiratory and maxillary odontogenic infections were in the early differential — “infections such as sinusitis, and facial or orbital cellulitis, as well as upper respiratory and maxillary odontogenic infections, would be included in the differential.” 5. Intracranial infections, mass lesions, and cavernous sinus thrombosis were considered with cranial neuropathies — “If neurologic findings are present, then one must consider intracranial infections, mass lesions and cavernous sinus thrombosis.” 6. Rhinocerebral mucormycosis emerged as most consistent with the rapid progression in an immunosuppressed, acidotic patient — “The diagnosis of invasive fungal rhino-orbito cerebral mucormycosis became only suspected with development of proptosis, chemosis, vision loss and bilateral ophthalmoplegia.”

selection.screen_reason: Rapid orbital swelling, ophthalmoplegia, vision loss and pansinus disease in a steroid-treated patient with DKA make rhino-orbital mucormycosis reachable.
selection.second_look_note: Rapid orbital swelling, vision loss and ophthalmoplegia with pansinus disease in a patient on chronic prednisone with diabetic ketoacidosis make rhino-orbital mucormycosis reachable.
